items.title: Herb Ellis interviewed by Michael Woods, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: when he needed a guitarist for his group, he asked for me.

ctx.x: Good, good. Tell us how you got started working with probably one of the greatest trios in all of jazz — Oscar Peterson and Ray Brown.

I was playing, I had been with bands, I’d been with Jimmy Dorsey, and the three of us in Jimmy Dorsey’s band, the bassist and the pianist and myself formed a trio, sort of a la Nat Cole, and we were playing in Buffalo. And we played in the same hotel for, oh months at a time. And the people from Canada, there was no liquor in Canada on Sundays at that time, but they’d come over for the music. And a lot of them came. And one night they brought Oscar Peterson with them. And he sat in and played with us and then…
You know that says something about musicians striking a certain chemistry.

items.title: Herb Ellis interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 16, 2000 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: I think certainly playing with Oscar and Ray was a highlight.

ctx.x: What kind of challenge was that musically in that group?

Oh my gosh it’s hard to describe. We had a lot of arrangements and they weren’t just charts that you’ve got a head, they were really complicated. And you had to remember them all, because we didn’t write it down. And Oscar made, he didn’t purposely make it — but he used to know about how much Ray and I could play, and he’d give us right up to the hilt.

items.title: Oscar Peterson interviewed by Joe Williams, Majesty of the Seas, May 31, 1995
items.q: Many of his recording feature the legendary trio with Ray Brown and Barney Kessel (later Herb Ellis and Ed Thigpen).

ctx.x: From his recording debut at age 19, Canadian pianist Oscar Peterson has built a career that is unrivaled in the history of jazz. Mr. Peterson’s astounding technique and melodic inventiveness have placed him at the forefront of modern jazz pianists. Many of his recording feature the legendary trio with Ray Brown and Barney Kessel (later Herb Ellis and Ed Thigpen). His frequent visits to the recording studio have also yielded wonderful pairings with artists such as Count Basie, Dizzy Gillespie, Louis Armstrong and…

I am pleased indeed to be seated at the foot of the king — at the feet of the one and only Mr. Oscar Peterson. He has no idea how I feel about him, really, because I kid him, pretend that we are equals, but he’s the king, really. He is the king. Oscar, this thing that we are doing, we are trying to preserve for the younger generation, some of the history of our music — how we were inspired, who inspired us, and all of that.
